analysis.investment_thesis: Aavas Financiers is building a genuine franchise in India's semi-urban and rural affordable housing market — a segment that commercial banks actively avoid — posting 22% revenue CAGR and 29.7% net profit CAGR over 7 years. ROE of 13.9% is still below my ideal threshold, but the underserved market opportunity and consistent profit compounding merit patient observation.
key_strengths: 29.7% net profit CAGR over 7 years (INR 93 Cr FY18 → INR 574 Cr FY25) — this is the kind of sustained earnings compounding I look for
Semi-urban/rural focus creates a genuine competitive barrier: competitors lack the branch infrastructure, local knowledge, and informal income assessment capabilities Aavas has built over a decade
High-quality institutional backing (FII: 24.72%, strong DIIs) validates the franchise; P/E of 21.8x and forward P/E of 13.6x is reasonable for this growth trajectory
key_risks: ROE of 13.9% and ROCE of 9.91% remain materially below Fisher's 20% ROE threshold — returns on capital must improve as the book seasons
Debt/Equity of 3.08 and total borrowings of INR 13,918 Cr create meaningful interest rate and credit cycle sensitivity in an economically volatile rural customer base
Revenue growth decelerated to flat in FY25 (INR 2,018 Cr FY24 → INR 1,988 Cr FY25) — any sustained deceleration would undermine the growth thesis
red_flags: FY25 finance cost data (INR 5 Cr vs INR 828 Cr in FY24) appears anomalous — likely a reporting classification issue, but warrants scrutiny of actual financial statements
OCF negative in all 5 years — entirely capital-markets dependent for growth funding
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Aavas has built something Fisher genuinely respects: a specialized franchise serving customers that larger institutions cannot profitably serve. The scuttlebutt on Aavas would reveal a company with deep local networks, proprietary income assessment for self-employed borrowers, and field-based origination that is difficult to replicate quickly. Net profit has compounded at 29.7% annually for 7 years — one of the cleaner growth records in Indian financial services.

The hold thesis rests on two gaps: ROE at 13.9% has not yet crossed 20%, and the FY25 revenue pause raises questions about whether competitive intensity or asset quality stress is emerging. I would want to see ROE trajectory toward 16-18% over the next 2 years and confirmation that the FY25 revenue pause was transient before upgrading to a strong buy. The forward P/E of 13.6x provides a reasonable entry margin if the growth thesis re-accelerates.
